newsitem.title: USA: Northeast wants Conn. deregulation in 2003.
newsitem.headline: Northeast wants Conn. deregulation in 2003.

text.p: Northeast Utilities said Tuesday it is proposing full competition in Connecticut's power market by the year 2003 -- a slower timetable than the state's attorney general is advocating.
The utility said it is urging state legislators to begin phasing in electricity deregulation in 1998, with the process to be completed in 2003.
"If we just open the door (in 1998), how do customers know what they're looking for?" Northeast spokeswoman Myra Humphries told Reuters in an interview.

Northeast is also proposing that its past investments or stranded costs of up to $3 billion be refinanced through the issuing of rate-reduction bonds, said Richard Soderman, director of regulatory planning at Northeast.
The costs include heavy debt from the utility's idled Millstone nuclear plants in Waterford, Conn.
The refinancing by 12-15-year bonds would allow Northeast subsidiary Connecticut Light & Power Co. (CL&P) to cut its rates by five percent, said Soderman.
CL&P has 6,000 employees and 1.1 million customers in Connecticut.
Electricity deregulation is expected to be a contentious issue in the current state legislative session which ends in early June.
The state has yet to take an official position on the timetable, but Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal is urging a much faster process.
Blumenthal told Reuters on Tuesday that Northeast's proposals were "woefully inadequate."
"We believe that competition can be achieved by 1998, and that their plan would put Connecticut first in costs and last in competition compared to many other states."

Blumenthal said that deregulation was the top item on his agenda. "The high cost of electric power in this state -- 30 percent above the national average -- is driving business away, and depressing our economy," he said.

"They are proposing in effect a much-delayed phase-in, with a pilot program involving a minute fraction of Connecticut consumers at the beginning, and no guarantee that full competition will be reached by 2003," said Blumenthal.
"And in the meantime, Connecticut consumers will finance their recovery of stranded costs," Blumenthal said, adding he was opposed to this.

But Northeast said securitization or refinancing of its existing costs was the best path. "It addresses two key issues," said Humphries. "One is immediate rate relief for all customers. The second is protection of our shareholders in recovery of strandable costs. Securitization accomplishes both of those, and is good for everybody."

"We would issue or create new rate-reduction bonds, and create a trust to oversee all this," she said. "This entails no obligation by the state. These are not state-backed, these are not tax-exempt. It will require legislation to create this trust and issue these bonds."
"We would use that immediate payback from the bond sale to pay off these investments on the books," said Humphries. "We would use that money to immediately lower rates for customers."

"Basically it's an interest-rate arbitrage in that the rate-reduction bonds carry a much lower borrowing cost than a utilities embedded cost of debt -- and that's where the big savings come from," added Soderman.
"We think that we can get about a five percent or perhaps more savings, or lower rates, as a direct result of this refinancing." --Matthew Lewis, Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224
